addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- claude-security:claude-security: The dedicated Claude Security orchestrator. Hand it an unattended job — "fully scan this repository and patch what you find; I understand it will use a lot of tokens" — and it runs the whole thing itself: capturing the revision, driving the multi-agent scan through the claude-security:scan workflow, assembling the verified report, and turning survivors into targeted patch files you apply when you choose, each verified by a panel of agents before it is written. Best as the main agent of a session. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Write, Edit, AskUserQuestion, Workflow, Workflow(claude-security:scan), TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskUpdate, TaskOutput, TaskStop, Agent(claude-security:scan-inventory, claude-security:scan-researcher, claude-security:scan-verifier, claude-security:patch-generator, claude-security:patch-verifier, claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:explore: Read-only code explorer that the plugin's other agents dispatch to map a codebase — locate files, trace how a flow is wired, find every caller of a symbol, answer "where does X happen". (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)

- claude-security:patch-generator: Implements the fix for one finding inside a scratch workspace clone, staged for review and delivery as a patch file; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Edit, Write, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:patch-verifier: The single verifier per fix round — reviews the workspace's staged diff against the finding, runs the tests, and states the three confidence claims a patch file must earn; dispatched by the fix job, not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:scan-inventory: Restricted read-only repository cartographer dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to partition the tree into components and account for every top-level directory; not for direct invocation or vulnerability research. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- claude-security:scan-researcher: Restricted read-only vulnerability researcher dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow; not for direct invocation or general exploration. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- claude-security:scan-verifier: Restricted read-only verifier dispatched by the Claude Security scan workflow to vote on one candidate finding; not for direct invocation. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Agent(claude-security:explore))

- code-review: Reviews the current branch diff plus every staged, unstaged, and untracked file, as an expert in the languages and frameworks this repository uses. Invoked at step 8 of the development workflow in AGENTS.md, before every commit, and again before opening a pull request if the reviewed state changed. Returns actionable findings with a confidence score; does not modify code. (Tools: Bash, Read, Glob, Grep)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- ui-review: Reviews changes as an expert in website design, usability, responsiveness, and accessibility. Invoked at step 6 of the development workflow in AGENTS.md, after an implementation pass and before the verifier. Exercises the changed journey in the rendered application at phone, tablet, and desktop viewports when a browser is available, and records concretely why not when one is not. Does not modify code. (Tools: Bash, Read, Glob, Grep, ToolSearch, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_navigate, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_resize, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_snapshot, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_take_screenshot, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_click, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_press_key, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_hover, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_evaluate, mcp__plugin_playwright_playwright__browser_console_messages)

- verifier: Runs the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for a change, then reports failures, flakes, missing coverage, and environment issues. Invoked at step 7 of the development workflow in AGENTS.md, after ui-review and before code-review. Give it the change scope (which surfaces were touched) if you know it; it will detect the scope itself otherwise. (Tools: Bash, Read, Glob, Grep)

Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- claude-code-setup:claude-automation-recommender: Analyze a codebase and recommend Claude Code automations (hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, MCP servers). Use when user asks for automation recommendations, wants to optimize their Claude Code setup, mentions improving Claude Code workflows, asks how to first set up Claude Code for a project, or wants to know what Claude Code features they should use.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.content:
1	# AGENTS
2	
3	This repository contains two runtime surfaces:
4	
5	- `apps/web/` for the Next.js web app (UI + API routes).
6	- `services/chat/` for the FastAPI chat service.
7	
8	Use this file as the default runbook for coding agents.
9	
10	## Source of truth
11	
12	`AGENTS.md` is the canonical format for agent instructions. The root file defines
13	repository-wide policy; a nested `AGENTS.md` adds authoritative instructions for
14	its subtree. Apply both, from the root down to the file closest to the work.
15	
16	Assistant-specific context files are pointers only. They contain no independent
17	instructions:
18	
19	| Assistant | Pointer file | Points at |
20	| --- | --- | --- |
21	| Claude Code | `CLAUDE.md` (per scope) | sibling `AGENTS.md` |
22	| Gemini CLI | `GEMINI.md` (per scope) | sibling `AGENTS.md` |
23	| GitHub Copilot | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | root `AGENTS.md` |
24	
25	Scopes with their own runbook:
26	
27	- `AGENTS.md` (repo-wide)
28	- `apps/web/AGENTS.md`
29	- `services/chat/AGENTS.md`
30	- `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`
31	
32	Never add instructions to a pointer file. That includes memories captured by pressing
33	`#` in Claude Code, which append to the nearest `CLAUDE.md` — move that text into the
34	matching `AGENTS.md` instead.
35	
36	`make agent-docs-check` (part of `make docs-check`, and gated in CI) fails when a
37	pointer drifts and prints the added lines. To restore the pointers locally after
38	moving the content across:
39	
40	```bash
41	make agent-docs-check FIX=1
42	```
43	
44	## Code Review Rules
45	
46	- Treat changes at system seams as one contract. When a change touches the web/chat
47	  payload, Prisma schema and handwritten SQL, dependency manifests and constraints,
48	  or container inputs and runtime files, inspect and validate both sides.
49	- Require guards to measure effective behavior, not a nearby declaration. Reject
50	  vacuous loops, mislabeled samples, or configuration checks that never exercise the
51	  rendered pixels, served bytes, accessibility tree, resolved files, or tool output
52	  named by the assertion.
53	- For runtime and container changes, verify the built artifact and real integration
54	  path. Unit tests cannot prove that a file was copied into an image, a service starts
55	  with its deployed configuration, or the web/chat/database path works together.
56	
57	## Development workflow
58	
59	Follow these steps in order for every change.
60	
61	1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
62	   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
63	   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.
64	
65	2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
66	   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
67	   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
68	   `main` state.
69	
70	3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a tracked issue or
71	   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
72	   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
73	   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer. If the next issue is too
74	   large for one pull request, split it into ordered slices and complete only
75	   the current slice. Keep pull requests small enough for thorough review,
76	   reliable verification, and quick rollback.
77	
78	4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
79	   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
80	   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
81	   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
82	   - Run focused tests while iterating.
83	   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.
84	
85	   **A guard added for behavior that already works has no red phase**, so the
86	   confirm-it-fails bullet never reaches it. Write down which mistake each
87	   assertion catches, and which ones nothing catches, then demonstrate it:
88	   break an input on purpose and watch that assertion fail on it. Coverage
89	   argued rather than demonstrated is the defect the guard was added to
90	   prevent, one level up.
91	
92	   **Measure what was produced, not what was asked for.** A guard that reads a
93	   declaration is measuring the request, and the two come apart constantly: a
94	   colour Tailwind serialises as `lab()` reads as a different colour through a
95	   regex for numbers; `ring-0` leaves its colour in the computed box-shadow
96	   with no geometry to paint it; a zero-width border still reports a border
97	   colour; a blurred shadow reports its source colour while every pixel it
98	   paints is composited toward the background; `outlineWidth` reports the
99	   user-agent default of `3px` for an outline whose style is `none`. Every one
100	   of those passed a check that looked right and was measuring something
101	   adjacent to the claim. Read the rendered pixels, the served bytes, the
102	   accessibility tree — whatever the asserted thing actually is.
103	
104	   The same trap catches fixtures and samples. Assert that a sample is what its
105	   name says — for example, a brightness band, an overlap, or a count that only
106	   the intended case produces. Fixture-isolation rules for the root guard suite
107	   live in `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`.
108	
109	   **Run the focused test here, and only the focused test.** This step needs
110	   the one spec or module under change, its red phase, and the mutations that
111	   demonstrate what each assertion catches. The `verifier` will not do those:
112	   it is instructed not to modify the repository, so breaking an input on
113	   purpose is not available to it. Fast whole-suite runners are fine too where
114	   they are genuinely fast — `make test-web` is a few seconds.
115	
116	   The one spec may itself be a journey, and then it needs a composed stack:
117	   `make e2e-smoke KEEP_STACK=1` builds one and leaves it up, and steps 6 and 7
118	   will want that same one. No make target runs a single spec, so running just
119	   the one is `npx playwright test <file>` from `apps/web`.
120	
121	   What does not belong here is the whole journey suite. Running it costs
122	   minutes per iteration, and the trigger for handing over is "I believe this
123	   is done", not "I want to know whether it works".
124	
125	5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
126	   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
127	   preserving work that belongs to the user. A real problem found here is filed
128	   as an issue before the change is removed — see *Unrelated findings become
129	   issues* below.
130	
131	6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
132	   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
133	   sub-agent must act as an expert in website design, usability,
134	   responsiveness, and accessibility. Address every actionable finding before
135	   running the `verifier`. For UI-affecting changes, exercise the changed
136	   journey in the rendered application at representative phone, tablet, and
137	   desktop viewports; inspect interaction, loading, empty, error, focus,
138	   keyboard, contrast, and responsive states as applicable; and capture
139	   screenshots or equivalent visual evidence.
140	
141	   A viewport is a width in CSS pixels, which says nothing about how many
142	   device pixels fill it. Where the change affects what the browser requests —
143	   anything carrying a `srcset`, or a source whose dimensions changed —
144	   exercise it at **2x as well as 1x**. Density is a property of the browser
145	   context (`deviceScaleFactor: 2`), not a width, so it needs a second pass
146	   rather than another viewport. A 2x screen asks for twice the CSS width, and
147	   the optimiser never upscales past the source, so a source that satisfies 1x
148	   can fall short at 2x while every 1x measurement stays clean. The 600px
149	   re-encode first tried in #152 came out at −0.9 to −2.2 dB PSNR at 1x and
150	   −4.4 to −6.6 dB at 2x: a difference at 1x small enough to accept, and one at
151	   2x that was plainly visible.
152	
153	   A change is UI-affecting when it moves a rendering dependency, too —
154	   `tailwindcss`, `next`, `react`, `postcss`, or a UI library in
155	   `apps/web/package.json`. That diff touches no component and can still change
156	   every rendered pixel; a Tailwind major shipped here with every check green.
157	
158	   For changes with no UI impact, explicitly record that rendered UI review is
159	   not applicable. If a finding is not applicable, record the concrete reason
160	   rather than silently ignoring it.
161	
162	   `ui-review` may start and stop a stack of its own. If one is already up —
163	   from step 4, or from an earlier pass through steps 6 and 7 when step 8 sends
164	   you back here — give it the `E2E_BASE_URL` and the ports if they are not the
165	   defaults, say the stack is not to be torn down, and say it is not
166	   `ui-review`'s. Naming it without addressing it is not a handover: remapped
167	   ports are normal here, and a reviewer that cannot reach the stack starts its
168	   own or renders nothing. Otherwise step 7's handover below promises a stack
169	   that stopped existing here.
170	
171	7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to run
172	   the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the
173	   change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage, and
174	   environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
175	   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
176	   rerun the verifier after addressing it.
177	
178	   **The whole battery belongs here** — the merge-gate command, the production
179	   build, the root guard suite, and the full journey run. Do not pre-run those
180	   and hand over a summary: it doubles the wall-clock, and a summary is not
181	   what the next step needs.
182	
183	   **Hand over the stack rather than leaving one to be found.** Where journeys
184	   need a composed stack, step 4 has usually built one, and step 6 may have
185	   built its own — `ui-review` is allowed to, and that one is then its to tear
186	   down and may be on ports it chose. Give the `E2E_BASE_URL`, say the stack is
187	   yours, and say `KEEP_STACK=1`: without that flag `make e2e-smoke` deletes
188	   the containers and their volumes on exit. What the handover buys is not the
189	   rebuild, which happens either way, but that the verifier knows a stack
190	   exists, knows where it is, and knows not to destroy it. Tear it down after
191	   the last step that needs it, not after this one.
192	
193	   Say the ports if they are not the defaults. `make test-e2e` follows
194	   `E2E_BASE_URL` anywhere; `make e2e-smoke` probes `127.0.0.1:3100` and
195	   `:8100` literally and cannot be aimed elsewhere, so it and a remapped stack
196	   do not mix. One of the ways they fail is a green smoke run against an
197	   unrelated project's containers, which is worse than a failure because
198	   nothing looks wrong. Exactly which way you get depends on which compose
199	   files resolve and which ports are already held, and is not worth predicting
200	   here. Free the default ports before step 7, or hand over nothing and say
201	   why.
202	
203	8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
204	   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
205	   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
206	   frameworks used by this application. Address every actionable finding
207	   before committing. If review findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate
208	   tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh `code-review` approval for the
209	   changed state.
210	
211	   That loop has no natural end, so ask for one: **have the reviewer say which
212	   findings are defects and which are refinements.** The loop ends on a round
213	   returning no defects, however many refinements come with it. Apply those,
214	   rerun the focused tests and the `verifier`, and record what was applied — a
215	   refinement-only change does not earn a fresh review round, here or at
216	   step 10.
217	
218	   **A fix made in this loop can invalidate step 6 as well.** If it alters what
219	   a page renders, rerun `ui-review` before the verifier and carry its verdict
220	   forward; the screenshots from step 6 otherwise describe a state that no
221	   longer exists. If it does not, record that the fix was not UI-affecting and
222	   go straight to the verifier. Only defects reopen step 6, on the same
223	   reasoning that ends this loop — a refinement applied to a rendered surface
224	   does not.
225	
226	9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
227	   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:
228	
229	   ```text
230	   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
231	   ```
232	
233	   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
234	   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.
235	
236	10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
237	    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
238	    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
239	      pre-commit review.
240	    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
241	      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
242	    - Except refinements the reviewer classified as such and step 8 cleared:
243	      applying those does not re-arm this, or the loop step 8 just ended
244	      reopens here.
245	    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
246	      remain unchanged.
247	    - Updating the branch from `main` — rebase, merge, or conflict resolution —
248	      invalidates **verification** as well as review. The builds, merge gates,
249	      smoke, and journeys were measured against a tree that no longer exists,
250	      so rerun step 7's applicable commands against the updated one rather than
251	      rerunning `code-review` alone.
252	    - Tear down any stack steps 4, 6, or 7 left running, once step 8's loop has
253	      closed and no further `verifier` run is coming: `make down`, or
254	      `docker compose down --volumes` to drop the seeded database with it. Step
255	      7 hands its stack forward under `KEEP_STACK=1`, which disables the only
256	      teardown the workflow otherwise performs — so without this the containers
257	      outlive the change and hold ports 3100, 55432, and 8100 against the next
258	      one.
259	    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
260	      required code review are complete.
261	    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open
262	      draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.
263	
264	11. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
265	    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never bypass
266	    a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed when these
267	    conditions are met. Use squash merge for short-lived development branches
268	    to keep `main` linear, then delete the merged branch.
269	
270	### Unrelated findings become issues
271	
272	Work turns up problems that are not the problem being worked on. A stale script,
273	a pre-existing overflow, a check that does not check what it claims. This can
274	happen at any step, and most often happens during steps 6 to 8, because
275	`ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` read more of the repository than the
276	change touches.
277	
278	**File an issue at the moment of finding, before deciding what to do about it.**
279	The finding is cheapest to write down while the context that produced it is
280	still loaded, and an issue costs little if it later turns out to be nothing.
281	
282	Two failure modes this exists to prevent, and they pull in opposite directions:
283	
284	- **Silently widening the change.** Fixing it here inflates a reviewed diff with
285	  work nobody scoped, and buries an independent decision inside an unrelated
286	  pull request.
287	- **Silently dropping it.** Mentioning it only in a review comment or a chat
288	  reply means it is gone as soon as that context is. Nobody rediscovers it until
289	  it breaks something.
290	
291	Filing an issue is what makes "not now" different from "never".
292	
293	Write enough that it can be acted on without rediscovering it: what is wrong,
294	where, how it was found, and why it was not fixed at the time. Include the
295	measurement if there was one. Link the issue from the pull request that surfaced
296	it, so the reviewer can see the finding was handled rather than missed.
297	
298	Fix it in the current change only when leaving it would make that change wrong
299	or unverifiable — a pre-existing problem the change makes materially worse, or a
300	check that has to work for this change to be trustworthy. That is a judgement
301	call, so state the reason in the commit message. When in doubt, file and leave
302	it: a separate pull request is cheap, and an unscoped one is not.
303	
304	Sub-agents report findings; they do not file issues. Every finding they report
305	that falls outside the current change needs the main agent to file it.
306	
307	### Sub-agents this workflow depends on
308	
309	Steps 6 through 8 use `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review`, defined in
310	`.claude/agents/`. All three run unattended: they cannot ask a question, and
311	they are instructed not to modify the repository they assess. That is an
312	instruction rather than a sandbox — each of them has `Bash` — so if a review
313	round is followed by working-tree changes you did not make, check `git status`
314	before assuming they are yours.
315	
316	**Their findings are claims, not verdicts.** Check the ones a change depends
317	on. This workflow has had a rendered review call a compliant focus indicator
318	"completely invisible" — acted on, it produced a guard that rejected a correct
319	design — and the same review quote a contrast ratio the running build measured
320	differently, zinc-400 at 2.56:1 against a measured 2.62:1. Both were believed
321	before they were checked. Address every finding, and where one is wrong, say so
322	with the measurement rather than complying.
323	
324	Record a disputed finding where someone else can audit it, and note when:
325	carried into the body of the commit step 9 is about to make, or into the pull
326	request body when the dispute arises after committing. Neither surface exists
327	while step 8 is running, so this is a commitment about what gets written, not a
328	precondition to satisfy first. Step 8's loop ends on a round returning no
329	defects, and a defect disputed rather than fixed counts as cleared only if it
330	is written down that way — a commit whose body omits it means step 8 did not
331	clear. Otherwise "I checked, it was wrong" lives inside one agent's reasoning,
332	and the gate opens with nothing to inspect.
333	
334	If one is unavailable — a different assistant, or a session started before the
335	definitions landed — carry out that step's intent directly and say which agent
336	was unavailable, rather than skipping the step or reporting it as done.
337	
338	`ui-review` needs a browser to satisfy step 6's rendered-journey requirement.
339	Where none is installed it falls back to reviewing source and must say so; a
340	review that claims viewports it never rendered is worse than none.
341	
342	## Repo map
343	
344	- `apps/web/src/app/`: Next.js pages and API routes.
345	- `apps/web/src/components/`: UI components.
346	- `apps/web/src/lib/`: shared web helpers and domain logic.
347	- `apps/web/Makefile`: web-owned dev/test/build command surface.
348	- `apps/web/AGENTS.md`: web-scoped agent runbook.
349	- `services/chat/src/api/`: chat service API and chat logic.
350	- `services/chat/tests/`: chat unit tests. Integration coverage lives in
351	  `scripts/e2e_smoke.py`, which runs against a real stack.
352	- `services/chat/Makefile`: chat-owned dev/test command surface.
353	- `services/chat/AGENTS.md`: chat-scoped agent runbook.
354	- `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`: fixture and mutation rules for root guard tests.
355	- `apps/web/prisma/`: shared data model and migrations.
356	- `infrastructure/`: deployment scripts and Terraform.
357	- `docs/`: operator and architecture docs.
358	
359	## Toolchain baseline
360	
361	- Node.js `22`
362	- Python `3.11`
363	
364	Use `mise` at repo root before running setup/CI commands:
365	
366	```bash
367	mise install
368	```
369	
370	### Python virtualenv
371	
372	All Python runs from a single project virtualenv at `.venv` (git-ignored). Make
373	targets create it on demand and invoke `.venv/bin/python` directly, so there is
374	nothing to activate — `make test-scripts`, `make quick-ci-chat`, and friends all
375	work from a clean shell.
376	
377	```bash
378	make venv
379	```
380	
381	Never install project Python dependencies into a system or mise interpreter. If
382	you run Python by hand, use `.venv/bin/python`, not `python`/`python3`.
383	
384	`PYTHON_BASE` is the interpreter used to *create* the venv (default
385	`mise exec python@3.11 -- python`); CI overrides it with `PYTHON_BASE=python`.
386	Do not override `PYTHON` itself — that bypasses the venv.
387	
388	## Canonical commands
389	
390	Run from repository root:
391	
392	```bash
393	make help
394	make bootstrap
395	make venv
396	make toolchain-doctor
397	make env-contract-check
398	make agent-doctor
399	make env-init
400	make setup            # web dependencies only — see the note below
401	make setup-chat
402	make setup-chat-full
403	make local-provider-check
404	make diagnose-chat-local
405	make docker-init-fresh
406	make prisma-generate
407	make migrate-deploy
408	make migrate NAME=add-order-status
409	make dev
410	make down
411	make test
412	make test-scripts
413	make quick-ci
414	make quick-ci-chat
415	make quick-ci-changed
416	make test-e2e
417	make e2e-smoke
418	make e2e-smoke-lite
419	make e2e-smoke-full
420	make release-dry-run
421	make docs-check
422	make agent-docs-check
423	make ci
424	```
425	
426	Unified npm command surface (root `package.json`):
427	
428	```bash
429	npm run bootstrap
430	npm run doctor
431	npm run env-contract-check
432	npm run setup         # web + chat — not the same as `make setup`
433	npm run setup:chat
434	npm run setup:chat:full
435	npm run local-provider-check
436	npm run diagnose:chat:local
437	npm run dev:web
438	npm run dev:chat
439	npm run test:scripts
440	npm run quick-ci
441	npm run quick-ci:changed
442	npm run quick-ci:chat
443	npm run e2e:smoke
444	npm run e2e:smoke:lite
445	npm run e2e:smoke:full
446	npm run release:dry-run
447	npm run docs:check
448	npm run agent-docs:check
449	npm run ci:web
450	npm run ci:chat
451	npm run ci
452	```
453	
454	The two `setup` entries are not the same command. `make setup` installs web
455	dependencies only; `npm run setup` runs `setup:web` then `setup:chat`. Use
456	`make bootstrap` when you want both through make, and reach for `make setup-chat`
457	if you already ran `make setup` and the chat imports are missing.
458	
459	Useful split commands:
460	
461	```bash
462	make dev-web
463	make dev-chat
464	make test-web
465	make test-chat
466	make docs-check
467	make -C apps/web help
468	make -C services/chat help
469	```
470	
471	## Environment files
472	
473	- Root app template: `.env.example`
474	- Chat service template: `services/chat/.env.example`
475	- Required keys contract: `config/env_contract.json`
476	- Required keys docs: `docs/ENV_CONTRACT.md`
477	
478	Copy templates to `.env` before local development.
479	
480	## Change boundaries
481	
482	- If you change web API payloads for chat, validate both:
483	  - `apps/web/src/app/api/chat/*`
484	  - `services/chat/src/api/*`
485	- If you change Prisma schema, run migrations and validate both web/chat tests.
486	  State whether the migration is destructive — a dropped or renamed column, a
487	  `NOT NULL` added to an existing one, a narrowed type. Local checks cannot tell
488	  you: they build the database fresh and seed it, so there is no data to lose and
489	  no older reader still running. Deployment has both.
490	  `infrastructure/scripts/docker-entrypoint.sh` applies migrations at container
491	  start while the previous revision is still serving, and rollback is a traffic
492	  shift back to that revision — which a destructive migration has already made
493	  unservable. Split those across two releases, expand then contract, or say in
494	  the pull request why this one does not need it.
495	- Prefer keeping generated artifacts and local runtime outputs out of commits.
496	
497	## Validation expectations
498	
499	Use `make quick-ci-changed` during implementation, and rerun it against an
500	explicit range when validating committed work:
501	
502	```bash
503	CHANGED_BASE=<base-sha> CHANGED_HEAD=<head-sha> make quick-ci-changed
504	```
505	
506	Every changed surface's merge-gate command has to have run before pushing.
507	Step 7 is where that happens, so this matrix is what tells `verifier` which
508	ones apply rather than a list to work through by hand:
509	
510	- Web: `make -C apps/web ci` (includes lint, type-check, tests, and build)
511	- Chat: `make -C services/chat ci`
512	- Scripts/tooling: `make test-scripts`
513	- Documentation/runbooks: `make docs-check`
514	- Cross-surface or repository-wide: `make ci`
515	
516	Add integration confidence where the change crosses a runtime boundary. These
517	are the verifier's too.
518	
519	- End-to-end journeys: `make test-e2e` (needs a running stack and the Playwright
520	  browser; see step 7)
521	- Cross-surface integration confidence: `make e2e-smoke`
522	- Contract-only integration confidence (minimal chat stack): `make e2e-smoke-lite`
523	- Full local-provider integration confidence: `make e2e-smoke-full`
524	- Release preflight: `make release-dry-run RELEASE_TAG=vX.Y.Z`
525	
526	## Troubleshooting
527	
528	- Toolchain mismatch: run `mise install`, then `make toolchain-doctor`.
529	- Virtualenv missing, broken, or on the wrong Python: run `rm -rf .venv && make venv`.
530	- `ModuleNotFoundError` for a chat dependency: you are probably outside the venv — re-run through `make`, or use `.venv/bin/python`. If you are inside it, the chat dependencies were never installed: `make setup` covers web only, so run `make setup-chat`.
531	- Playwright journeys fail with a missing browser: run `make -C apps/web install-e2e-browsers`, then rerun `make test-e2e`. Neither `make setup` nor `make bootstrap` installs it.
532	- Env contract drift: run `make env-contract-check` and update contract/templates/docs together.
533	- Docs link drift (including root runbooks): run `make docs-check`.
534	- Agent doc drift (a `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, or `.github/copilot-instructions.md` gained content): move the flagged lines into the matching `AGENTS.md`, then run `make agent-docs-check FIX=1`.
535	- Release guardrail failure: run `make release-dry-run` and fix missing guardrail files.
536	- E2E smoke failure: run `make e2e-smoke KEEP_STACK=1`, then inspect `docker compose logs`.
537	- Need local LLM/vector dependencies in Docker chat image: rerun with `CHAT_INSTALL_LOCAL_STACK=1`.
538	- Need local LLM/vector dependencies in Python chat setup: run `make setup-chat-full`.
539	- Need one-command local-provider preflight checks: run `make local-provider-check`.
540	- Need fuller local chat diagnostics (preflight + health payload + compose logs): run `make diagnose-chat-local`.
541	- Need to initialize a fresh Docker DB volume and rebuild chat product index: run `make docker-init-fresh`.
542	- Local-provider startup preflight fails (`LLM_PROVIDER=local`): start Ollama (`ollama serve`), pull model (`ollama pull <LOCAL_MODEL_NAME>`), and for docker chat use `OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434`.
543	- Full-profile smoke failure in CI: inspect `e2e-full-compose.log`, `e2e-full-metrics.txt`, `e2e-full-metrics-summary.md`, `e2e-full-dependencies-health.json`, and `e2e-full-alert-state.md` artifacts.
544	- Scheduled full-profile smoke alerts keep one open issue per alert class and auto-close when scheduled runs recover; include run URL and summary when triaging.
545	- Missing env files: run `make env-init`, then update `.env` and `services/chat/.env`.
546	- Sandbox-only build failure (`listen EPERM`): run `make ci` outside restricted sandbox.
547	
548	## Building and running
549	
550	Follow the validation matrix above. `make quick-ci-changed` is the iteration loop,
551	not a substitute for the applicable merge-gate command. Web merge gates include a
552	production build through `make -C apps/web ci` or `make ci`.
553	
554	When doing git operations use the GitHub CLI `gh` where possible.
555	
556	## Git repo
557	
558	The main branch for this project is called `main`.
559	
560	## Comments policy
561	
562	Only write high-value comments if at all. Avoid talking to the user through comments.
563	
564	## General style requirements
565	
566	Use hyphens instead of underscores in flag names (e.g. `my-flag` instead of `my_flag`).
567	
568	JavaScript/TypeScript and React conventions live in `apps/web/AGENTS.md`.

# AGENTS

This repository contains two runtime surfaces:

- `apps/web/` for the Next.js web app (UI + API routes).
- `services/chat/` for the FastAPI chat service.

Use this file as the default runbook for coding agents.

## Source of truth

`AGENTS.md` is the canonical format for agent instructions. The root file defines
repository-wide policy; a nested `AGENTS.md` adds authoritative instructions for
its subtree. Apply both, from the root down to the file closest to the work.

Assistant-specific context files are pointers only. They contain no independent
instructions:

| Assistant | Pointer file | Points at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `CLAUDE.md` (per scope) | sibling `AGENTS.md` |
| Gemini CLI | `GEMINI.md` (per scope) | sibling `AGENTS.md` |
| GitHub Copilot | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` | root `AGENTS.md` |

Scopes with their own runbook:

- `AGENTS.md` (repo-wide)
- `apps/web/AGENTS.md`
- `services/chat/AGENTS.md`
- `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`

Never add instructions to a pointer file. That includes memories captured by pressing
`#` in Claude Code, which append to the nearest `CLAUDE.md` — move that text into the
matching `AGENTS.md` instead.

`make agent-docs-check` (part of `make docs-check`, and gated in CI) fails when a
pointer drifts and prints the added lines. To restore the pointers locally after
moving the content across:

```bash
make agent-docs-check FIX=1
```

## Code Review Rules

- Treat changes at system seams as one contract. When a change touches the web/chat
  payload, Prisma schema and handwritten SQL, dependency manifests and constraints,
  or container inputs and runtime files, inspect and validate both sides.
- Require guards to measure effective behavior, not a nearby declaration. Reject
  vacuous loops, mislabeled samples, or configuration checks that never exercise the
  rendered pixels, served bytes, accessibility tree, resolved files, or tool output
  named by the assertion.
- For runtime and container changes, verify the built artifact and real integration
  path. Unit tests cannot prove that a file was copied into an image, a service starts
  with its deployed configuration, or the web/chat/database path works together.

## Development workflow

Follow these steps in order for every change.

1. **Inspect before changing anything.** Inspect the repository, current Git
   state, and all applicable instruction files before making changes. Preserve
   unrelated staged, unstaged, and untracked work.

2. **Create a branch first.** Create a dedicated feature, fix, refactor, chore,
   test, or documentation branch before making code changes. Never commit
   directly to `main`, and create the branch from the latest appropriate
   `main` state.

3. **Choose a thin vertical slice.** Before implementing a tracked issue or
   feature, define the smallest end-to-end slice that can be reviewed, tested,
   shipped, and merged independently. Prefer one coherent user-visible or
   operational outcome over a broad horizontal layer. If the next issue is too
   large for one pull request, split it into ordered slices and complete only
   the current slice. Keep pull requests small enough for thorough review,
   reliable verification, and quick rollback.

4. **Use test-driven development when behavior or structure is testable.**
   - Add or update a focused test before implementation.
   - Run it and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
   - Implement the smallest appropriate change.
   - Run focused tests while iterating.
   - Refactor only while the relevant tests remain green.

   **A guard added for behavior that already works has no red phase**, so the
   confirm-it-fails bullet never reaches it. Write down which mistake each
   assertion catches, and which ones nothing catches, then demonstrate it:
   break an input on purpose and watch that assertion fail on it. Coverage
   argued rather than demonstrated is the defect the guard was added to
   prevent, one level up.

   **Measure what was produced, not what was asked for.** A guard that reads a
   declaration is measuring the request, and the two come apart constantly: a
   colour Tailwind serialises as `lab()` reads as a different colour through a
   regex for numbers; `ring-0` leaves its colour in the computed box-shadow
   with no geometry to paint it; a zero-width border still reports a border
   colour; a blurred shadow reports its source colour while every pixel it
   paints is composited toward the background; `outlineWidth` reports the
   user-agent default of `3px` for an outline whose style is `none`. Every one
   of those passed a check that looked right and was measuring something
   adjacent to the claim. Read the rendered pixels, the served bytes, the
   accessibility tree — whatever the asserted thing actually is.

   The same trap catches fixtures and samples. Assert that a sample is what its
   name says — for example, a brightness band, an overlap, or a count that only
   the intended case produces. Fixture-isolation rules for the root guard suite
   live in `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`.

   **Run the focused test here, and only the focused test.** This step needs
   the one spec or module under change, its red phase, and the mutations that
   demonstrate what each assertion catches. The `verifier` will not do those:
   it is instructed not to modify the repository, so breaking an input on
   purpose is not available to it. Fast whole-suite runners are fine too where
   they are genuinely fast — `make test-web` is a few seconds.

   The one spec may itself be a journey, and then it needs a composed stack:
   `make e2e-smoke KEEP_STACK=1` builds one and leaves it up, and steps 6 and 7
   will want that same one. No make target runs a single spec, so running just
   the one is `npx playwright test <file>` from `apps/web`.

   What does not belong here is the whole journey suite. Running it costs
   minutes per iteration, and the trigger for handing over is "I believe this
   is done", not "I want to know whether it works".

5. **Inspect the complete diff.** Review the branch diff plus all staged,
   unstaged, and untracked files. Remove accidental or unrelated changes while
   preserving work that belongs to the user. A real problem found here is filed
   as an issue before the change is removed — see *Unrelated findings become
   issues* below.

6. **Run `ui-review` before verification.** After the main agent completes an
   implementation pass, invoke the `ui-review` sub-agent. The `ui-review`
   sub-agent must act as an expert in website design, usability,
   responsiveness, and accessibility. Address every actionable finding before
   running the `verifier`. For UI-affecting changes, exercise the changed
   journey in the rendered application at representative phone, tablet, and
   desktop viewports; inspect interaction, loading, empty, error, focus,
   keyboard, contrast, and responsive states as applicable; and capture
   screenshots or equivalent visual evidence.

   A viewport is a width in CSS pixels, which says nothing about how many
   device pixels fill it. Where the change affects what the browser requests —
   anything carrying a `srcset`, or a source whose dimensions changed —
   exercise it at **2x as well as 1x**. Density is a property of the browser
   context (`deviceScaleFactor: 2`), not a width, so it needs a second pass
   rather than another viewport. A 2x screen asks for twice the CSS width, and
   the optimiser never upscales past the source, so a source that satisfies 1x
   can fall short at 2x while every 1x measurement stays clean. The 600px
   re-encode first tried in #152 came out at −0.9 to −2.2 dB PSNR at 1x and
   −4.4 to −6.6 dB at 2x: a difference at 1x small enough to accept, and one at
   2x that was plainly visible.

   A change is UI-affecting when it moves a rendering dependency, too —
   `tailwindcss`, `next`, `react`, `postcss`, or a UI library in
   `apps/web/package.json`. That diff touches no component and can still change
   every rendered pixel; a Tailwind major shipped here with every check green.

   For changes with no UI impact, explicitly record that rendered UI review is
   not applicable. If a finding is not applicable, record the concrete reason
   rather than silently ignoring it.

   `ui-review` may start and stop a stack of its own. If one is already up —
   from step 4, or from an earlier pass through steps 6 and 7 when step 8 sends
   you back here — give it the `E2E_BASE_URL` and the ports if they are not the
   defaults, say the stack is not to be torn down, and say it is not
   `ui-review`'s. Naming it without addressing it is not a handover: remapped
   ports are normal here, and a reviewer that cannot reach the stack starts its
   own or renders nothing. Otherwise step 7's handover below promises a stack
   that stopped existing here.

7. **Run `verifier` before code review.** Invoke the `verifier` sub-agent to run
   the builds, static checks, tests, and journey coverage appropriate for the
   change. The verifier must report failures, flakes, missing coverage, and
   environment issues. Fix or explicitly resolve every actionable finding
   before starting code review. If a verifier finding requires a code change,
   rerun the verifier after addressing it.

   **The whole battery belongs here** — the merge-gate command, the production
   build, the root guard suite, and the full journey run. Do not pre-run those
   and hand over a summary: it doubles the wall-clock, and a summary is not
   what the next step needs.

   **Hand over the stack rather than leaving one to be found.** Where journeys
   need a composed stack, step 4 has usually built one, and step 6 may have
   built its own — `ui-review` is allowed to, and that one is then its to tear
   down and may be on ports it chose. Give the `E2E_BASE_URL`, say the stack is
   yours, and say `KEEP_STACK=1`: without that flag `make e2e-smoke` deletes
   the containers and their volumes on exit. What the handover buys is not the
   rebuild, which happens either way, but that the verifier knows a stack
   exists, knows where it is, and knows not to destroy it. Tear it down after
   the last step that needs it, not after this one.

   Say the ports if they are not the defaults. `make test-e2e` follows
   `E2E_BASE_URL` anywhere; `make e2e-smoke` probes `127.0.0.1:3100` and
   `:8100` literally and cannot be aimed elsewhere, so it and a remapped stack
   do not mix. One of the ways they fail is a green smoke run against an
   unrelated project's containers, which is worse than a failure because
   nothing looks wrong. Exactly which way you get depends on which compose
   files resolve and which ports are already held, and is not worth predicting
   here. Free the default ports before step 7, or hand over nothing and say
   why.

8. **Run `code-review` before every commit.** Invoke the `code-review`
   sub-agent against the current branch diff and every staged, unstaged, and
   untracked file. The reviewer must act as an expert in the languages and
   frameworks used by this application. Address every actionable finding
   before committing. If review findings cause changes, rerun the appropriate
   tests and the `verifier`, then obtain a fresh `code-review` approval for the
   changed state.

   That loop has no natural end, so ask for one: **have the reviewer say which
   findings are defects and which are refinements.** The loop ends on a round
   returning no defects, however many refinements come with it. Apply those,
   rerun the focused tests and the `verifier`, and record what was applied — a
   refinement-only change does not earn a fresh review round, here or at
   step 10.

   **A fix made in this loop can invalidate step 6 as well.** If it alters what
   a page renders, rerun `ui-review` before the verifier and carry its verdict
   forward; the screenshots from step 6 otherwise describe a state that no
   longer exists. If it does not, record that the fix was not UI-affecting and
   go straight to the verifier. Only defects reopen step 6, on the same
   reasoning that ends this loop — a refinement applied to a rendered surface
   does not.

9. **Commit after approval.** Commit only after verification and code review
   are complete. Use Conventional Commits:

   ```text
   <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
   ```

   Keep the subject at 72 characters or fewer, describe why in the body when
   useful, and do not combine unrelated work.

10. **Create pull requests from the reviewed state.**
    - Confirm that local verification remains valid.
    - Rerun `code-review` only if the reviewed state changed after the
      pre-commit review.
    - A changed state includes code, tests, documentation, generated files,
      conflict resolution, or any other staged, unstaged, or untracked content.
    - Except refinements the reviewer classified as such and step 8 cleared:
      applying those does not re-arm this, or the loop step 8 just ended
      reopens here.
    - Do not repeat code review when the already-reviewed diff and worktree
      remain unchanged.
    - Updating the branch from `main` — rebase, merge, or conflict resolution —
      invalidates **verification** as well as review. The builds, merge gates,
      smoke, and journeys were measured against a tree that no longer exists,
      so rerun step 7's applicable commands against the updated one rather than
      rerunning `code-review` alone.
    - Tear down any stack steps 4, 6, or 7 left running, once step 8's loop has
      closed and no further `verifier` run is coming: `make down`, or
      `docker compose down --volumes` to drop the seeded database with it. Step
      7 hands its stack forward under `KEEP_STACK=1`, which disables the only
      teardown the workflow otherwise performs — so without this the containers
      outlive the change and hold ports 3100, 55432, and 8100 against the next
      one.
    - Push and create the pull request only after local verification and any
      required code review are complete.
    - Open a normal, ready-for-review pull request by default. Do not open
      draft pull requests unless the user explicitly asks for a draft.

11. **Merge only clean, passing pull requests.** Merge only after GitHub
    reports a clean merge state and every configured check passes. Never bypass
    a failing or pending required check. Self-merges are allowed when these
    conditions are met. Use squash merge for short-lived development branches
    to keep `main` linear, then delete the merged branch.

### Unrelated findings become issues

Work turns up problems that are not the problem being worked on. A stale script,
a pre-existing overflow, a check that does not check what it claims. This can
happen at any step, and most often happens during steps 6 to 8, because
`ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review` read more of the repository than the
change touches.

**File an issue at the moment of finding, before deciding what to do about it.**
The finding is cheapest to write down while the context that produced it is
still loaded, and an issue costs little if it later turns out to be nothing.

Two failure modes this exists to prevent, and they pull in opposite directions:

- **Silently widening the change.** Fixing it here inflates a reviewed diff with
  work nobody scoped, and buries an independent decision inside an unrelated
  pull request.
- **Silently dropping it.** Mentioning it only in a review comment or a chat
  reply means it is gone as soon as that context is. Nobody rediscovers it until
  it breaks something.

Filing an issue is what makes "not now" different from "never".

Write enough that it can be acted on without rediscovering it: what is wrong,
where, how it was found, and why it was not fixed at the time. Include the
measurement if there was one. Link the issue from the pull request that surfaced
it, so the reviewer can see the finding was handled rather than missed.

Fix it in the current change only when leaving it would make that change wrong
or unverifiable — a pre-existing problem the change makes materially worse, or a
check that has to work for this change to be trustworthy. That is a judgement
call, so state the reason in the commit message. When in doubt, file and leave
it: a separate pull request is cheap, and an unscoped one is not.

Sub-agents report findings; they do not file issues. Every finding they report
that falls outside the current change needs the main agent to file it.

### Sub-agents this workflow depends on

Steps 6 through 8 use `ui-review`, `verifier`, and `code-review`, defined in
`.claude/agents/`. All three run unattended: they cannot ask a question, and
they are instructed not to modify the repository they assess. That is an
instruction rather than a sandbox — each of them has `Bash` — so if a review
round is followed by working-tree changes you did not make, check `git status`
before assuming they are yours.

**Their findings are claims, not verdicts.** Check the ones a change depends
on. This workflow has had a rendered review call a compliant focus indicator
"completely invisible" — acted on, it produced a guard that rejected a correct
design — and the same review quote a contrast ratio the running build measured
differently, zinc-400 at 2.56:1 against a measured 2.62:1. Both were believed
before they were checked. Address every finding, and where one is wrong, say so
with the measurement rather than complying.

Record a disputed finding where someone else can audit it, and note when:
carried into the body of the commit step 9 is about to make, or into the pull
request body when the dispute arises after committing. Neither surface exists
while step 8 is running, so this is a commitment about what gets written, not a
precondition to satisfy first. Step 8's loop ends on a round returning no
defects, and a defect disputed rather than fixed counts as cleared only if it
is written down that way — a commit whose body omits it means step 8 did not
clear. Otherwise "I checked, it was wrong" lives inside one agent's reasoning,
and the gate opens with nothing to inspect.

If one is unavailable — a different assistant, or a session started before the
definitions landed — carry out that step's intent directly and say which agent
was unavailable, rather than skipping the step or reporting it as done.

`ui-review` needs a browser to satisfy step 6's rendered-journey requirement.
Where none is installed it falls back to reviewing source and must say so; a
review that claims viewports it never rendered is worse than none.

## Repo map

- `apps/web/src/app/`: Next.js pages and API routes.
- `apps/web/src/components/`: UI components.
- `apps/web/src/lib/`: shared web helpers and domain logic.
- `apps/web/Makefile`: web-owned dev/test/build command surface.
- `apps/web/AGENTS.md`: web-scoped agent runbook.
- `services/chat/src/api/`: chat service API and chat logic.
- `services/chat/tests/`: chat unit tests. Integration coverage lives in
  `scripts/e2e_smoke.py`, which runs against a real stack.
- `services/chat/Makefile`: chat-owned dev/test command surface.
- `services/chat/AGENTS.md`: chat-scoped agent runbook.
- `tests/scripts/AGENTS.md`: fixture and mutation rules for root guard tests.
- `apps/web/prisma/`: shared data model and migrations.
- `infrastructure/`: deployment scripts and Terraform.
- `docs/`: operator and architecture docs.

## Toolchain baseline

- Node.js `22`
- Python `3.11`

Use `mise` at repo root before running setup/CI commands:

```bash
mise install
```

### Python virtualenv

All Python runs from a single project virtualenv at `.venv` (git-ignored). Make
targets create it on demand and invoke `.venv/bin/python` directly, so there is
nothing to activate — `make test-scripts`, `make quick-ci-chat`, and friends all
work from a clean shell.

```bash
make venv
```

Never install project Python dependencies into a system or mise interpreter. If
you run Python by hand, use `.venv/bin/python`, not `python`/`python3`.

`PYTHON_BASE` is the interpreter used to *create* the venv (default
`mise exec python@3.11 -- python`); CI overrides it with `PYTHON_BASE=python`.
Do not override `PYTHON` itself — that bypasses the venv.

## Canonical commands

Run from repository root:

```bash
make help
make bootstrap
make venv
make toolchain-doctor
make env-contract-check
make agent-doctor
make env-init
make setup            # web dependencies only — see the note below
make setup-chat
make setup-chat-full
make local-provider-check
make diagnose-chat-local
make docker-init-fresh
make prisma-generate
make migrate-deploy
make migrate NAME=add-order-status
make dev
make down
make test
make test-scripts
make quick-ci
make quick-ci-chat
make quick-ci-changed
make test-e2e
make e2e-smoke
make e2e-smoke-lite
make e2e-smoke-full
make release-dry-run
make docs-check
make agent-docs-check
make ci
```

Unified npm command surface (root `package.json`):

```bash
npm run bootstrap
npm run doctor
npm run env-contract-check
npm run setup         # web + chat — not the same as `make setup`
npm run setup:chat
npm run setup:chat:full
npm run local-provider-check
npm run diagnose:chat:local
npm run dev:web
npm run dev:chat
npm run test:scripts
npm run quick-ci
npm run quick-ci:changed
npm run quick-ci:chat
npm run e2e:smoke
npm run e2e:smoke:lite
npm run e2e:smoke:full
npm run release:dry-run
npm run docs:check
npm run agent-docs:check
npm run ci:web
npm run ci:chat
npm run ci
```

The two `setup` entries are not the same command. `make setup` installs web
dependencies only; `npm run setup` runs `setup:web` then `setup:chat`. Use
`make bootstrap` when you want both through make, and reach for `make setup-chat`
if you already ran `make setup` and the chat imports are missing.

Useful split commands:

```bash
make dev-web
make dev-chat
make test-web
make test-chat
make docs-check
make -C apps/web help
make -C services/chat help
```

## Environment files

- Root app template: `.env.example`
- Chat service template: `services/chat/.env.example`
- Required keys contract: `config/env_contract.json`
- Required keys docs: `docs/ENV_CONTRACT.md`

Copy templates to `.env` before local development.

## Change boundaries

- If you change web API payloads for chat, validate both:
  - `apps/web/src/app/api/chat/*`
  - `services/chat/src/api/*`
- If you change Prisma schema, run migrations and validate both web/chat tests.
  State whether the migration is destructive — a dropped or renamed column, a
  `NOT NULL` added to an existing one, a narrowed type. Local checks cannot tell
  you: they build the database fresh and seed it, so there is no data to lose and
  no older reader still running. Deployment has both.
  `infrastructure/scripts/docker-entrypoint.sh` applies migrations at container
  start while the previous revision is still serving, and rollback is a traffic
  shift back to that revision — which a destructive migration has already made
  unservable. Split those across two releases, expand then contract, or say in
  the pull request why this one does not need it.
- Prefer keeping generated artifacts and local runtime outputs out of commits.

## Validation expectations

Use `make quick-ci-changed` during implementation, and rerun it against an
explicit range when validating committed work:

```bash
CHANGED_BASE=<base-sha> CHANGED_HEAD=<head-sha> make quick-ci-changed
```

Every changed surface's merge-gate command has to have run before pushing.
Step 7 is where that happens, so this matrix is what tells `verifier` which
ones apply rather than a list to work through by hand:

- Web: `make -C apps/web ci` (includes lint, type-check, tests, and build)
- Chat: `make -C services/chat ci`
- Scripts/tooling: `make test-scripts`
- Documentation/runbooks: `make docs-check`
- Cross-surface or repository-wide: `make ci`

Add integration confidence where the change crosses a runtime boundary. These
are the verifier's too.

- End-to-end journeys: `make test-e2e` (needs a running stack and the Playwright
  browser; see step 7)
- Cross-surface integration confidence: `make e2e-smoke`
- Contract-only integration confidence (minimal chat stack): `make e2e-smoke-lite`
- Full local-provider integration confidence: `make e2e-smoke-full`
- Release preflight: `make release-dry-run RELEASE_TAG=vX.Y.Z`

## Troubleshooting

- Toolchain mismatch: run `mise install`, then `make toolchain-doctor`.
- Virtualenv missing, broken, or on the wrong Python: run `rm -rf .venv && make venv`.
- `ModuleNotFoundError` for a chat dependency: you are probably outside the venv — re-run through `make`, or use `.venv/bin/python`. If you are inside it, the chat dependencies were never installed: `make setup` covers web only, so run `make setup-chat`.
- Playwright journeys fail with a missing browser: run `make -C apps/web install-e2e-browsers`, then rerun `make test-e2e`. Neither `make setup` nor `make bootstrap` installs it.
- Env contract drift: run `make env-contract-check` and update contract/templates/docs together.
- Docs link drift (including root runbooks): run `make docs-check`.
- Agent doc drift (a `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md`, or `.github/copilot-instructions.md` gained content): move the flagged lines into the matching `AGENTS.md`, then run `make agent-docs-check FIX=1`.
- Release guardrail failure: run `make release-dry-run` and fix missing guardrail files.
- E2E smoke failure: run `make e2e-smoke KEEP_STACK=1`, then inspect `docker compose logs`.
- Need local LLM/vector dependencies in Docker chat image: rerun with `CHAT_INSTALL_LOCAL_STACK=1`.
- Need local LLM/vector dependencies in Python chat setup: run `make setup-chat-full`.
- Need one-command local-provider preflight checks: run `make local-provider-check`.
- Need fuller local chat diagnostics (preflight + health payload + compose logs): run `make diagnose-chat-local`.
- Need to initialize a fresh Docker DB volume and rebuild chat product index: run `make docker-init-fresh`.
- Local-provider startup preflight fails (`LLM_PROVIDER=local`): start Ollama (`ollama serve`), pull model (`ollama pull <LOCAL_MODEL_NAME>`), and for docker chat use `OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434`.
- Full-profile smoke failure in CI: inspect `e2e-full-compose.log`, `e2e-full-metrics.txt`, `e2e-full-metrics-summary.md`, `e2e-full-dependencies-health.json`, and `e2e-full-alert-state.md` artifacts.
- Scheduled full-profile smoke alerts keep one open issue per alert class and auto-close when scheduled runs recover; include run URL and summary when triaging.
- Missing env files: run `make env-init`, then update `.env` and `services/chat/.env`.
- Sandbox-only build failure (`listen EPERM`): run `make ci` outside restricted sandbox.

## Building and running

Follow the validation matrix above. `make quick-ci-changed` is the iteration loop,
not a substitute for the applicable merge-gate command. Web merge gates include a
production build through `make -C apps/web ci` or `make ci`.

When doing git operations use the GitHub CLI `gh` where possible.

## Git repo

The main branch for this project is called `main`.

## Comments policy

Only write high-value comments if at all. Avoid talking to the user through comments.

## General style requirements

Use hyphens instead of underscores in flag names (e.g. `my-flag` instead of `my_flag`).

JavaScript/TypeScript and React conventions live in `apps/web/AGENTS.md`.

Durable context for whoever — or whatever — picks this up next. Kept as an issue rather than in an agent's local memory so it survives a cleared context and is visible to everyone.

## How this repository is being worked

Changes go through the [AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md) workflow end to end: branch, implement, ui-review, verifier, code-review, PR. PRs merge when CI is green. Findings become issues. The loop continues to the next item without pausing for step-by-step approval.

The point is that it runs unattended, so stopping to confirm each step defeats it.

## What still gets surfaced rather than decided silently

Proceeding by default does not mean deciding everything. Three categories get a recommendation and a question:

1. **Changes to what users see** — image quality, layout tradeoffs. #96 is the live example: re-encoding to WebP is well-measured, but q82/600px is a judgment about acceptable fidelity, not a fact.
2. **Changes to other contributors' behavior** — #147 committed tool config that runs hooks on anyone's machine who clones. That deserved saying out loud, not just doing.
3. **Rewrites of shared history** — never silently. See the note below on why this keeps coming up.

The rest of the work does not wait on those answers. Finish everything that does not depend on the decision first, then ask.

## Two things that have repeatedly caught people out

**Checks that run without asserting on what they produced.** This is the repo's signature defect, found three separate times: the E2E smoke passed against a chat service returning `fallback: true`; the seed ran green on every PR while writing credentials that could never authenticate (#141); a category page referenced an image that had never existed (#137). A green check is not evidence unless something inspects its output.

**Verifying in a richer environment than the real one.** Also recurring: a populated local venv vs CI's bare one; jsdom vs a real browser; three sampled viewports vs the breakpoint boundaries where the defects actually live; `node_modules` vs the standalone image; a local stack reading `.env` vs CI with none. If a check passes locally, confirm it runs in the environment that matters.

**Deleting files does not shrink `git clone`.** The blobs stay reachable from history. #146 removed 68.6 MB from the working tree and the web image; `size-pack` did not move. Worth remembering before promising a clone-size win — see the measurement in #66.

## Running the stack locally

Environments differ per machine (port collisions, whether Ollama is installed for `LLM_PROVIDER=local`). `make e2e-smoke` may need a compose override for ports and provider. Resolve collisions with an override file using `ports: !override` — a plain `ports:` list appends rather than replaces — and never by stopping containers you did not start.

## Current state

`main` is clean. #145, #146 and #147 are merged. Open: #96 (WebP re-encode, the next substantive item), #66 (image weight, parent of #96), #118 (import-declaration guardrail), #129 (chat panel below `sm`, needs a design decision), #69 and #90 (blocked upstream).

title:	The chat panel cannot be opened under next dev, only in a production build
state:	OPEN
author:	scottdensmore (Scott Densmore)
labels:	bug
comments:	0
assignees:	
projects:	
milestone:	
issue-type:	
parent:	
sub-issues:	
sub-issues-completed:	
blocked-by:	
blocking:	
number:	228
--
Hit repeatedly while working #196 and #216, and worth writing down because it silently costs a review pass every time.

## What happens

`npx next dev` on a free port, click the launcher, and nothing opens:

```
launcher visible: true
#chat: 0   dialog: 0   aside/section: 0
launcher still there: 1
pageerrors: (none)
```

Reproduced on two independently started dev servers. Against a composed production stack the same click opens the panel and `chat-controls.spec.ts` passes 2/2, so this is `next dev` specifically, not the code being broken.

React *is* hydrated on the dev server — a controlled input on `/contact` keeps its typed value, and `window.next` is present — so this is not a general hydration failure. It is this component.

## Likely mechanism

`apps/web/src/components/chat.tsx:217-230` closes the panel whenever focus moves outside the widget:

```ts
const onFocusIn = (event: FocusEvent) => {
  const target = event.target as Node | null
  if (target && widgetRef.current?.contains(target)) return
  closedByFocusOut.current = true
  setShowChat(false)
}
```

Opening the panel unmounts the launcher (#190), so the focused element disappears and focus falls to `document.body`. `body` is not inside `widgetRef`, so the handler closes the panel again. In a production build the panel's own autofocus wins that race; under dev — where React 19's StrictMode mounts effects, tears them down and mounts them again — it does not.

That last sentence is the part I have not proven. The behaviour is reproducible; the StrictMode explanation is the most likely cause and is untested. `reactStrictMode` is not set in `next.config.js`, so it defaults on.

## Why it matters more than it looks

Every chat journey is unrunnable locally without standing up docker. That is documented in `playwright.config.ts` as "these journeys cross web, chat and the database", which is true of the *message* path but not of this: opening a panel needs no backend. The real reason is this bug, and the comment hides it.

It also means `ui-review` cannot see the chat panel on a dev server, so any review of chat UI silently falls back to reading source. That happened twice today.

## Worth checking as part of a fix

Whether a focus landing on `document.body` should close the panel at all. `relatedTarget === null` or a `body` target is the browser losing focus rather than the user moving it somewhere, which is the same distinction the comment above that effect already draws for the address bar.
